Five new countries — Federated States of Micronesia (FM), Marshall Islands (MH), Palau (PW), Greenland (GL) and Puerto Rico (PR) — plus two new US nodes the research forced (`gasb-standards`, `uscensus-acs`). FLAG FOR THOMAS: the second of those two mints overrides a prior session's explicit scope decision (it had deliberately withheld the Census ALFIN mint pending a full US local-government-finance pass) rather than resolving a gap in evidence — see that entry's own `why` field for the full reasoning; revert if the original scope discipline is preferred. reports.title: Governmental Accounting Standards Board standards (US GAAP for state and local government)
reports.description: The standard-setting body for US state and local government accounting, and the framework three sovereign Pacific states in free association with the United States report under. Minted this session because the research forced it: the corpus already held `ipsas` and Canada's `psab-psas`, and had no US public-sector equivalent, which made the single largest exporter of public-sector accounting method in this dataset invisible. Named in the compliance note of all three Compact states in identical wording.
reports.cadence_note: Statements are issued as numbered pronouncements several times a year rather than as a periodic publication; `releases_per_year` is an estimate of pronouncement cadence, not of a titled serial.

release_schedule.note: Rolling technical agenda, no fixed calendar. Effective-date lag after issuance of a standard ranges from about 8 months to over 4 years depending on the standard.

reports.title: American Community Survey
reports.description: The Census Bureau's continuous demographic and socio-economic survey, published in 1-year and 5-year data releases. Minted because Puerto Rico's certified fiscal plan cites it by exact product name and vintage — a distinct product from `uscensus-population-estimates`, which the corpus already holds, and conflating the two would have been the same error this project has twice had to correct in submitted research.
reports.cadence_note: 1-year and 5-year estimate releases annually; the 5-year file is the one cited by the Puerto Rico fiscal plan.

release_schedule.note: 2025 1-year estimate date undetermined as of this audit (2026-08-11) — Census is assessing a new disclosure-avoidance policy that already delayed the 5-year products ~7 weeks past their historical December pattern. Entries above are the last confirmed release, not a forward projection; worth re-checking before the next window.

reports.title: Financial Statements of the FSM National Government
reports.publisher: FSM National Government / Office of the National Public Auditor
reports.description: The audited whole-of-government financial statements of the Federated States of Micronesia, a sovereign state in free association with the United States. Reports on US GAAP with GASB named as standard-setter, audited by Ernst & Young LLP (Kolonia, Pohnpei) under US GAAS and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States. The document describes the FSM in its own words as "an independent sovereign nation" — which is what makes the wholesale adoption of another country's accounting framework worth recording rather than assuming.
reports.cadence_note: Annual, lagged: the FY2023 statements (year ended 30 September 2023) were signed and audited 22 December 2025, and the file itself is a January 2026 revision.

release_schedule.note: One financial-statement report is produced per fiscal year (FYE Sept 30), but the audit/release lag has been lengthening with no consistent month of release: FY2020 report dated 12.31.21 (~15mo lag), FY2021 dated 04.28.23 (~19mo lag), FY2022 dated 10.10.24 (~24mo lag), FY2023 dated 12.22.25/revised 01.28.26 (~28mo lag) — per the ONPA's own report index. No statutory deadline or calendar was found stating a fixed due date. As of 2026-08-11, no FY2024 statements have appeared yet, consistent with the widening lag; given the trend a next (FY2024) release might plausibly land sometime in 2027, but this is not a sourced date and is deliberately omitted as an entry.

reports.title: Financial Statements of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RepMar)
reports.publisher: Republic of the Marshall Islands / Office of the Auditor-General
reports.description: The audited whole-of-government financial statements of the Marshall Islands. Same framework as FSM and Palau, in near-identical wording. NOT AN INSTITUTION-EXPORT CASE, and the distinction matters for this corpus's audit census: the Marshall Islands has its own constitutionally independent Auditor-General — Constitution Article VIII § 15(1), "The Auditor-General shall audit the public funds and accounts of the Republic of the Marshall Islands...", § 15(5), "shall not receive any direction from the Cabinet or from any other authority or person, but shall act independently" — and the Single Audit fieldwork is contracted to Ernst & Young (RMI), Inc. of Majuro. So a foreign method arrives through a private firm, not through a foreign audit institution. Contrast Niue and Tokelau, where the New Zealand Auditor-General personally signs.
reports.cadence_note: Annual, heavily lagged: the FY2022 statements (year ended 30 September 2022) were issued 4 June 2025 — thirty-two months.

release_schedule.note: The RMI Office of the Auditor-General publishes RepMar's audited financial statements annually (one per fiscal year, FY ending Sept 30), but with a highly variable lag and no fixed release date or governing rule. Observed publication lags across the archive range from about 9 months (e.g. FY2016-FY2018, issued each following June) to 32 months (FY2022, issued 4 June 2025) and 28 months (FY2023, issued 29 January 2026), landing in nearly every month of the year (Jan, Feb, Mar, May, Jun, Nov, Dec across different fiscal years) with no consistent time-of-year pattern. The governing statute, the Auditor-General (Definition of Duties, Functions and Powers) Act 1986, requires only semi-annual reports to the Nitijela (at its January and August sessions, per section 903(1)) and gives audited agencies 15 days to respond to findings (section 909(1)) -- it sets no deadline for completing or releasing the annual financial statement audit itself. As of this research (11 Aug 2026), FY2023 is the latest published edition (issued 29 Jan 2026); FY2024 has not yet appeared, and given the historical lag range there is no way to compute a credible next date.

reports.title: Financial Statements of the Republic of Palau
reports.publisher: Republic of Palau / Office of the Public Auditor
reports.description: The audited whole-of-government financial statements of Palau. Carries the sharpest evidence in this corpus that an imported standard genuinely binds rather than being cited decoratively: the FY2022 opinion on governmental activities is QUALIFIED, and qualified specifically because Palau had not implemented GASB Statement No. 87 *Leases*. A jurisdiction can only fail a numbered standard of a foreign standard-setter if that standard-setter's pronouncements actually govern it. Audited by Ernst & Young (CNMI), Inc. of Koror.
reports.cadence_note: Annual, heavily lagged: the FY2022 statements (year ended 30 September 2022) were issued 2 October 2025 — thirty-six months.

release_schedule.note: No calendar or fixed rule governs the national ROP financial statements' release; the audit backlog lag varies year to year. FY2022 statements (FYE 30 Sep 2022) were issued 2 Oct 2025 (36-month lag, per existing cadence_note). Newly confirmed: FY2023 statements (FYE 30 Sep 2023) were issued 26 May 2026 by Ernst & Young (CNMI), Inc. (32-month lag) — see https://www.palauopa.org/pdf/single-audits/FY%202023/ROP-FY2023-FS_Final-05.26.26.pdf. As of 11 Aug 2026, no FY2024 ROP financial statements have been posted yet on the OPA single-audits page. The lag is shrinking slightly but remains multi-year and irregular in timing (Oct release vs. May release), so no fixed next-occurrence date can be computed.

reports.title: Landskassens Regnskab
reports.description: The annual accounts of the Landskasse, Greenland's central government treasury, presented to Inatsisartut. THE FIFTH DISTINCT ANSWER this project has now recorded to one question. Greenland names neither IPSAS (as the Cook Islands do), nor Danish state accounting rules, nor nothing at all (as Niue does), nor an undefined 'generally accepted accounting practice' (as Tokelau does), nor a foreign standard-setter (as the three Compact states do). It names its own legislature's statute and its own executive order. Audited by a private independent auditor, not by Denmark's Rigsrevisionen — so Greenland imports audit standards and imports no accounting framework at all.
reports.cadence_note: Annual and punctual, in sharp contrast to every other jurisdiction in this slice: the 2025 accounts were signed in Nuuk on 30 April 2026, four months after year-end.

entries.covers: Landskassens Regnskab 2025 (signed in Nuuk, presented as pkt. 11, FM2026)

release_schedule.note: Naalakkersuisut has signed the annual state accounts (landskassens regnskab) consistently in late April each year: 25 Apr 2024 (for FY2023), 30 Apr 2025 (for FY2024), and 30 Apr 2026 (for FY2025, filed as ina.gl pkt11_fm2026). The signed accounts are then presented to Inatsisartut at the spring session (Forårssamling). Separately, Inatsisartutlov nr. 26 af 28. november 2016 om kommunernes og Grønlands Selvstyres budgetter og regnskaber sets a statutory outer deadline requiring Naalakkersuisut to present a 'revideret' (audited) landskasseregnskab no later than Inatsisartut's autumn session (efterårssamling) for the preceding fiscal year — but actual practice runs well ahead of that backstop, with signing/spring-session presentation about 4 months after year-end. Next expected edition: FY2026 accounts, expected to be signed and presented around April 2027 (FM2027).

reports.title: Inatsisartutlov nr. 26 af 28. november 2016 om kommunernes og Grønlands Selvstyres budgetter og regnskaber
reports.description: Greenland's own budget and accounts statute, covering both the municipalities and the Self-Government, together with Selvstyrets bekendtgørelse nr. 6 af 20. januar 2022. This is the framework `gl-landskassens-regnskab` reports under and the framework the independent auditor's opinion is expressed against — a wholly self-legislated accounting basis in a jurisdiction inside another state's monetary and constitutional perimeter. Structurally it plays the role AASB 1049 plays for Australia or the CIPFA Code for the UK, except that nobody outside Greenland wrote it.
reports.cadence_note: A statute, amended rather than published on a schedule ('med senere ændringer' in the auditor's own reference).

release_schedule.note: This is a Greenlandic parliamentary act (Inatsisartutlov), not a recurring statistical/periodic publication. It has been amended irregularly by subsequent acts as legislative need arose: Inatsisartutlov nr. 24/2018, nr. 13/2021, and nr. 63/2023, and was most recently issued as a consolidated act (Selvstyrets lovbekendtgørelse nr. 83 af 04.12.2025) folding in those amendments. There is no calendar, no stated periodic-release rule, and no fixed interval pattern — amendments/consolidations occur whenever Inatsisartut legislates on the subject, not on a schedule.

reports.title: Certified Fiscal Plan for the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico
reports.publisher: Financial Oversight and Management Board for Puerto Rico (FOMB)
reports.description: The multi-year fiscal plan certified by the federal Oversight Board established under PROMESA (Pub. L. 114-187). The richest single document in either Realm slice for this corpus's purposes: it names external statistical releases by title and vintage in its macroeconomic sections, which almost nothing else in these two slices does. `jurisdiction_level` is `provincial` as the least-bad fit — Puerto Rico is a US territory whose fiscal plan is certified by a federally appointed board, and the corpus has no level for that.
reports.cadence_note: Certified periodically rather than annually, with revisions between vintages; the version read this session is the 2024 Fiscal Plan, 164 pages. Certified annual budgets are a separate document.

release_schedule.note: Under 48 U.S.C. § 2141 (PROMESA), the Oversight Board has sole discretion to set and change the schedule for Fiscal Plan development, submission, approval, certification, and revisions; the statute imposes no fixed date or fixed annual deadline, only that each certified Fiscal Plan must cover not less than 5 fiscal years from the year of certification. FOMB's own FAQ states the Fiscal Plan is 'updated at least annually' as a living document, but this is an aspirational minimum, not a dated rule or calendar — no month/day is specified. As of 2026-08-11, the Commonwealth Fiscal Plan on the publisher's page (oversightboard.pr.gov/fiscal-plans/) remains the 2024 vintage (the most recent Commonwealth entry listed), while other FOMB-covered entities (e.g., PREPA) have had newer plans certified in 2025 — confirming certification timing varies by entity/vintage rather than following a fixed schedule. This confirms the existing cadence_note's characterization of periodic (not annual, not calendar-based) certification.

reports.title: Government Auditing Standards (the Yellow Book)
reports.publisher: Comptroller General of the United States / US Government Accountability Office
reports.description: The United States' public-sector auditing standards, revised periodically and universally known as the Yellow Book. Minted because it is named by title and by issuing officer in the audit report of all three Compact states — the vehicle by which US audit method reaches three sovereign nations. Distinct from `gasb-standards`, which governs how the accounts are prepared: this governs how they are examined, and the two travel together but are not the same export.
reports.cadence_note: Revised roughly every three years (2011, 2018, 2024 revisions).

release_schedule.note: GAO revises Government Auditing Standards (Yellow Book) on an as-needed basis, not a fixed cycle. Past major revisions occurred in 1972, 1974, 1988, 1994, 2003, 2007, 2011, 2018 (with a 2021 technical update), and 2024 — gaps ranging from 2 to 13 years. The 2024 revision (GAO-24-106786) is the current edition, effective for periods beginning on or after December 15, 2025; GAO has not announced a date for the next revision. A December 2025 FAQ document (GAO-26-108710) is supplementary guidance on the 2024 edition's quality management requirements, not a new edition of the standards.

reports.title: Puerto Rico Oversight, Management, and Economic Stability Act (PROMESA)
reports.description: Pub. L. 114-187, codified at 48 U.S.C. ch. 20, the statute creating the Financial Oversight and Management Board and the fiscal-plan certification regime that currently structures Puerto Rico's public finances. Unusual among statutes in this corpus for specifying what the plan it mandates must be BASED ON — § 201(b)(1)(A) requires estimates "in conformance with agreed accounting standards" and grounded in applicable law, and § 201(b)(1)(H) requires the plan to "create independent forecasts of revenue". A federal statute imposing a methodology requirement, which is rare.
reports.cadence_note: A statute, amended rather than published on a schedule. Enacted 30 June 2016.

release_schedule.note: PROMESA (Public Law 114-187) is a one-off foundational statute enacted June 30, 2016, not a recurring report. It is amended irregularly by subsequent acts of Congress as needed (no fixed cadence, no calendar, no stated periodic-release rule for the Act's text itself). The Act does impose recurring reporting duties on entities it created (e.g., the Financial Oversight and Management Board's annual report due within 30 days of fiscal year end, and quarterly Governor submissions within 15 days of quarter end) — but those are separate reports issued by those bodies, not releases of PROMESA itself. Given this, releases_per_year should probably not be treated as a fixed number for this entry.

reports.title: Lov om Grønlands Selvstyre (Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009)
reports.description: Greenland's Self-Government Act, the Danish statute setting the constitutional and fiscal relationship between Denmark and Greenland. Its § 5 fixes the annual block grant (bloktilskud) at a real 2009 amount and indexes it; its § 8 reduces the grant by half of Greenland's mineral revenue above a threshold that is itself indexed the same way. Filed under `DK` because the publisher is the Danish Parliament, with `region` carrying the subject — the same convention the corpus uses elsewhere for a metropolitan statute governing a dependency.
reports.cadence_note: A statute, in force since 2009 and amended rather than reissued.

release_schedule.note: This is a statute (Act no. 473 of 12 June 2009, the Greenland Self-Government Act), not a periodic statistical release. It has been in force since 2009 and is amended by subsequent acts of the Folketing as needed, with no fixed schedule, stated periodicity rule, or observed regular pattern of reissuance. Confirms the existing cadence_note.

reports.title: Pris- og lønforudsætninger
reports.publisher: Økonomistyrelsen (Danish Agency for Public Finance and Management)
reports.description: The price and wage assumptions used to uprate the Danish Finance Act, published annually by Økonomistyrelsen as a table of named indices — Statsligt lønindeks, Forbrugerprisindeks, Nettoprisindeks, Anlægsindeks, Vejindeks and the Generelt pris- og lønindeks. Minted to settle a question two research rounds could not: the Greenland block grant is indexed to "det generelle pris- og lønindeks på finansloven", and it was unclear whether that index was a published series or a parameter internal to the budget. It is published, with a title, a publisher and an annual cadence — so the indexation clause is a real edge and not an unresolvable reference.
reports.cadence_note: Updated once a year, by June, for the following year's Finance Act proposal — the page read this session states "Pris- og lønforudsætninger er senest blevet opdateret d. 23. juni 2026" and "opdateres vanligt kun én gang årligt senest juni".

entries.covers: Annual update of price and wage assumptions

release_schedule.rule: Pris- og lønforudsætningerne opdateres vanligt kun én gang årligt senest juni. (Price and wage assumptions are ordinarily updated only once a year, by June at the latest.)
release_schedule.note: Page states assumptions were last updated 23 June 2026 and are ordinarily updated once annually no later than June. Since the 2026 update has already occurred as of 2026-08-11, the next expected update is by June 2027. Exact day within June is not specified by the publisher.

reports.title: Informe Económico a la Gobernadora y a la Asamblea Legislativa
reports.publisher: Puerto Rico Planning Board (Junta de Planificación)
reports.description: The Puerto Rico Planning Board's annual economic report to the Governor and Legislative Assembly, carrying the Board's own growth forecasts and a statistical appendix. Named directly by the Financial Oversight and Management Board's certified Fiscal Plan as a forecast it consults: 'The Oversight Board has consulted other economic forecasts in the process of preparing the Fiscal Plan forecasts – notably the forecasts of the Puerto Rico Planning Board's (PRPB)... The PRPB's projection of growth is higher than this Fiscal Plan forecast.' Minted 2026-08-09 (sweep session, Tier-3 item) closing a `no-node-yet` lead.
reports.cadence_note: Annual, addressed to the Governor and Legislative Assembly each year — the 2025 edition is titled 'Informe Económico a la Gobernadora y a la Asamblea Legislativa 2025'.

entries.covers: Informe Económico covering 2025 (reported by Metro PR on 2026-05-04)

release_schedule.note: No published release calendar or a clearly stated statutory deadline was locatable (jp.pr.gov blocks direct fetch via robots.txt/TLS from this environment, and no dated calendar page surfaced via search). Instead, dated PDF uploads of the report's accompanying Apéndice Estadístico plus news coverage show a consistent pattern: the edition covering calendar year N is released around May of year N+1 (e.g. Apéndice Estadístico 2022 uploaded jp.pr.gov 2023/05; Apéndice Estadístico 2023 uploaded jp.pr.gov 2024/05; the 2025 edition was covered by Puerto Rico press on 2026-05-04). Note the Board has a documented history of severe backlog for some years — e.g. the 2018-2020 editions were not uploaded until 2021-2023 — so single-year slippage of many months is plausible even though the modern pattern targets May.

reports.title: Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finances (ALFIN)
reports.description: The Census Bureau's own description: 'the only known comprehensive source of state and local government finance data collected on a nationwide scale using uniform definitions, concepts, and procedures,' authorized under Title 13, United States Code, and operating continuously since 1957. Cited by Puerto Rico's certified Fiscal Plan by exact title and vintage in the same footnote that carries the American Community Survey citation: 'Census – Annual Survey of State and Local Government Finance, 2021.' A distinct Census product from both `uscensus-acs` and `uscensus-population-estimates`. Minted 2026-08-09 (sweep session, Tier-3 item) — the original entry withheld this mint pending a broader US local-government-finance research pass 'so one node without its context would [not be] misleading'; minted anyway as an isolated, well-evidenced node with one documented edge already in hand (the same standard applied to fed-h15's Treasury yield-curve node and this project's other isolated mints this session), rather than waiting on unscoped future research.
reports.cadence_note: A census (full enumeration) is conducted every five years (years ending in '2' and '7'); a sample survey collects data in the intervening years, so the release is effectively annual.

entries.covers: 2023 State & Local Government Finance data release
2024 State & Local Government Finance data release
2025 State & Local Government Finance data (projected next annual release)

release_schedule.note: Census Bureau's ALFIN/gov-finances program page (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/gov-finances.html) shows the 2023 data vintage was released July 2025 and the 2024 data vintage was released July 2026 — a consistent one-year-later, July-release cadence (data for fiscal year N released in July of year N+2). The same page states 'The 2026 Annual Survey of Local Government Finance will be mailed November 2026,' confirming an ongoing annual collection cycle. No formal dated release calendar or statutory release rule was found, so this is inferred from the observed pattern of the last two vintages, not a published schedule.

_dropped.edge: AUDITS — the census, and what the 2026-08-06 schema decision did and did not fix
_dropped.why: SUPERSEDED IN PART, 2026-08-06, and the correction is more interesting than the original note. The census stands: the six documented instances separate into (1) EXPORT OF INSTITUTION, twice, both in the Realm — the Controller and Auditor-General of New Zealand signs Niue's accounts under Article 60 of NIUE'S OWN Constitution, and is installed as Tokelau's auditor by the Tokelau Finance Rules 1998; (2) EXPORT OF METHOD ONLY, three times, all in the Compact states — Ernst & Young entities in Kolonia, Majuro and Koror audit under US GAAS and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, while each state retains its own audit office (the Marshall Islands' is constitutionally independent under Article VIII § 15); (3) NEITHER, once — Greenland, where a private auditor works under international auditing standards plus 'de yderligere krav der er gældende i Grønland' and a Greenlandic statute. WHAT CHANGED: this note argued the blocker was the ontology, and on that argument `RelationType` ('audits', 'supersedes') and a parallel unweighted `relations` list were added to `src/lib/types.ts` on 2026-08-06 — see `notes/SCHEMA-DECISION-relationship-types.md`. Exactly ONE of the six instances became a relation: Niue, in `realm-government-finance.json`. WHAT DID NOT CHANGE, AND WHY THIS NOTE IS NOW FILED AS `unpublishable-source` RATHER THAN `note`: the four method-export and neither cases cannot be minted no matter what the type union says, because THE AUDITOR IS NOT A PUBLISHABLE RECURRING RELEASE. Ernst & Young Kolonia, Majuro and Koror are private firms whose opinions are bound into the audited statements themselves; Greenland's auditor likewise. That is `Research.1.md` §4.2's standing disqualifier, the same one that keeps J.D. Power, ICE Brent and Darroch Limited out of this corpus, and it is not a gap that a schema change can reach. The three `-> us-gao-yellow-book` dependencies already in this slice are the honest representation of the method export: what is documented and mintable is that the statements depend on the American auditing standard, not that a named private firm audits them. SO THE CORRECTED FINDING IS: the ontology gap was real and is now closed, but it was never the binding constraint. The binding constraint on representing assurance in this corpus is the node inventory, and specifically the rule that a node must be a recurrently published official report. Auditors mostly are not. Where a public audit office publishes recurrently — the Controller and Auditor-General of New Zealand does, which is why `nu-ag-report-assembly` exists — the relation is mintable; where the auditor is a private firm, it never will be. That is a structural fact about public-sector assurance and worth having as a finding rather than as a backlog item.
